# Best RV power station and solar combo

The right pick depends on whether you need to run a roof AC. A 13,500 BTU roof AC draws about 1,500 W and spikes past 3,000 W at startup, so it needs a 3,000 W+ unit ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).

## My picks

**1. Best value for a big RV setup: ALLPOWERS R4000**
- It has 3,456 Wh, 3,600 W continuous at 120 V, an RV outlet, and LiFePO4 cells rated for 3,500+ cycles.
- It accepts up to 2,000 W of solar across three 650 W inputs (12-60 V), so you can run a large rooftop array.
- The warranty is 5 years. It weighs 45 kg (about 99 lb), so it's a "stays in the bay" unit.
- The store price is $1,499. Code EXTRA12 took $179.88 off in a cart test on 2026-10-23, bringing it to $1,319.12. The code expires 2026-11-15 and needs an order over $1,200. Codes generally don't stack.
- Returns are 30 days if unused, and the buyer pays return shipping. The seller's refund page says sale items can't be returned.
- **[Buy the ALLPOWERS R4000](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh)** (affiliate link; the site earns a commission at no cost to you). Source: [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/allpowers-r4000-3456wh)

**2. Best for full-time boondocking: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3**
- It has 4,096 Wh (expandable past 12 kWh), 4,000 W continuous, and 8,000 W surge.
- It recharges 0-80% in about 50 minutes from a wall outlet. It's heavy, and it's the priciest once you add expansion batteries.
- Source: [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)

**3. Simplest for running AC: Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro**
- It has 3,024 Wh, 3,000 W continuous, and 6,000 W surge. That's enough to start a 13,500 BTU AC without a soft-start kit.
- Source: [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)

**4. Mid-range budget pick: BLUETTI AC200L**
- It has 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W, a built-in 30A RV port, and up to 1,200 W of solar input.
- It's best for fridge, lights, and electronics rather than AC. It weighs about 62 lb.
- Sources: [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/), [SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)

**5. Weekend trips: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 or EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus**
- The Jackery 1000 v2 has 1,070 Wh, weighs about 24 lb, and takes up to 400 W of solar. Two SolarSaga 200W panels use that full 400 W.
- The DELTA 3 Plus has 1,024 Wh and takes up to 1,000 W of solar. It's about 28 lb and expands to 5 kWh.
- Source: [SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)

## Pairing the panels
- **Match panels to the unit's solar input limit.** A big array on a low-input unit gets bottlenecked, a common mismatch in RV and van builds ([GetWattLogic](https://getwattlogic.com/articles/bluetti-vs-jackery-vs-ecoflow-van-life)).
- **Folding panels:** a 300-400 W array can refill a mid-size unit in a full day of decent sun ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)). Jackery's SolarSaga (100W/200W) and the Renogy 200W Foldable Solar Suitcase are named as pairings ([NomadSignal](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife)).
- **Rooftop:** the R4000's 650 W-per-input limit means each string must stay within its voltage and current range.

My search results didn't include direct purchase links for the panels or for the EcoFlow, Jackery, and Bluetti units. The review pages above carry their retailer links, so check current prices there.

## Caveats
- The sources don't always agree on specs. One older comparison lists the Bluetti AC200P with a 700 W solar cap, while the newer AC200L is listed at 1,200 W. Confirm specs on the manufacturer's page before buying.
- For any hardwired connection to the RV, use a licensed electrician. Plugging in via a TT-30 adapter is the simple route ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)). That article covers Ontario rules, so check local requirements.

If you tell me your RV's loads (AC, fridge, Starlink) and how many nights you boondock, I can narrow it to one unit and a panel wattage.
